newsitem.title: DUBAI: Letter bombs baffle Arabic newspaper.
newsitem.headline: Letter bombs baffle Arabic newspaper.

text.p: Bombs mailed to the British and U.S. offices of al-Hayat raise the question of who opposes an Arabic newspaper that boasts of objective coverage, interviewing everyone from a fiery Egyptian cleric to the Arab leaders he denounces as infidels.

Three letter bombs addressed to al-Hayat's United Nations bureau were found on Monday, hours after a bomb exploded at its London headquarters, wounding two security guards. British police said four more suspected devices were found.

Jihad Khazen, editor of the newspaper owned by a member of the Saudi royal family, said at the headquarters of the London-based newspaper there was no warning. "Nobody threatened us or demanded anything."

The letters at the United Nations were similar to those mailed earlier this month to the newspaper's Washington bureau. Its office in the Saudi capital Riyadh also received two letter bombs this month, a source close to al-Hayat told Reuters on Tuesday.

"Somebody is unhappy with what al-Hayat has been writing. But the suspect list should not just have militants. Arab governments who are unhappy with the fact that al-Hayat allows militants to air their views should also be added," said Jamal Khashoggi, the al-Hayat Jeddah bureau chief who covers Moslem militant movements across the Arab world.
He said he had been in recent contact with followers of Egyptian Sheikh Omar Abdel-Rahman, the blind cleric jailed in the United States for plotting to blow up New York City landmarks.
"They are unhappy about the letter bombs and condemned them," said Khashoggi, who has interviewed Abdel-Rahman twice.
He said al-Hayat interviewed militant leaders and published in-depth stories about their movements -- the kind of articles they would never see in the official Arabic press.
Al-Hayat has also published claims of responsibility for political violence and letters written by Moslem militant groups who are seeking to topple Arab governments.
However, Saudi analysts concede that al-Hayat does not give as extensive coverage to dissidents in Saudi Arabia, its largest market.
The newspaper is owned by Prince Khaled bin Sultan, son of the kingdom's powerful Defence Minister Prince Sultan and a nephew of King Fahd.

The Saudi royal family has been condemned by Moslem militants incensed by its tight alliance with Washington. Two bombings in Saudi Arabia have killed 24 Americans and rattled the kingdom. Four Saudi Moslem militants were beheaded for carrying out one of the attacks.
Asked if Moslem militants could have targeted al-Hayat because of its owner, managing editor Khairallah Khairallah said: "I cannot accuse anyone, we have no indications. It's a puzzle."
Khashoggi, who received a written threat two years ago, said the most radical Arab Islamist groups may have been angered by the newspaper.
"We have criticised the most radical groups. Groups like the ones in Algeria who slit the throat of someone only because they are related to an army officer," he said.
Al-Hayat has built a reputation as one of the most objective newspapers in the Arab world, navigating the region's political minefields while trying to maintain its credibility.
The newspaper has in the past been temporarily banned in Saudi Arabia and other Arab states where official publications devote much coverage to praising leaders and their activities.
"It is independent as much as there is independence. It's a breath of fresh air but it's risky for the paper to write political stories," said a Saudi political analyst.

The Lebanese founder of the newspaper, Kamel al-Mroweh, was assassinated in Beirut in 1966. It is printed in New York, London, Frankfurt, Bahrain and Cairo and has a global circulation of between 120,000 and 130,000.
The staff at its 20 bureaus worldwide have been told to remain alert and take precautions. A bomb detector has been installed in its London headquarters.
"The letter bombs will make us more determined to pursue our journalistic objectives with all our might," al-Hayat said in a front-page editorial on Tuesday.
